C1.title: Savings account
C1.summary: An account for holding money. Pays interest, limits withdrawals, and at big banks pays close to zero.
C1.hook: Your bank pays you 0.01% and lends your money out at 7%. That gap has a name: their profit.
sources: FDIC National Rates and Rate Caps (national average savings rate 0.38%

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A bank account built for holding money rather than spending it. No debit card for purchases, usually a limit on how many withdrawals per month, and it pays interest: the bank pays you a small percentage for leaving money there.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone keeping money aside for a goal or an emergency. Most people's first one is at the same bank as their checking.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The bank lends your deposits out at a much higher rate than it pays you. The FDIC's national average savings rate was 0.38% in August 2026, many large banks paid 0.01%, and competitive online accounts paid around 4%. That gap is the bank's profit.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Earning almost nothing without realizing better options exist. Monthly fees on some accounts if the balance drops.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the APY? Is there a minimum balance or a fee? How fast can I move money back to checking?

C10.title: Inflation
C10.summary: Why cash loses buying power, how it's measured, and what it does to every other station on this map.
C10.hook: Nobody takes money out of your account. It just buys less each year.
sources: September 2026: all-items index up 3.7% over the last 12 months (released October 14

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The general rise in prices over time, which means each dollar buys a little less. It's measured by indexes like the Consumer Price Index, a basket of goods and services priced every month. In September 2026 the CPI was up 3.7% from a year earlier. Inflation is the reason savings rates, loan rates, wages, and investment returns all get discussed as 'real' (after inflation) or 'nominal' (before).

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone, whether they think about it or not. It hits hardest on cash and fixed payments: a savings balance earning less than inflation shrinks in buying power, and a fixed pension or bond coupon buys less each year. It's kinder to people who owe fixed-rate debt, because they repay with cheaper dollars.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Nobody collects it directly. But a bank paying 0.4% on savings while prices rise 3.7% is paying you a negative real rate and lending the money out at a positive one. Any product that quotes a return without saying 'after inflation' is quoting the bigger number.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Keeping decades of savings in cash because it feels safe. Judging a raise or a return without subtracting inflation. Assuming the official index matches your own costs; rent and healthcare can run well above the headline number.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the inflation rate right now, and what does my savings account pay? What's the real return on this? Is this payment fixed for life, or does it adjust? What did the same thing cost five years ago?

C11.title: The Fed & interest rates
C11.summary: Who sets the rate that moves your savings APY, your card APR, and your mortgage, and how to read a rate decision.
C11.hook: Eight times a year, a committee sets one number. Your card, your savings, and your mortgage all move after it.
sources: 2026: target range raised 1/4 point to 3.75% to 4% · https://federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260916a.htm · 2026-09-16

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The Federal Reserve is the U.S. central bank. Its rate-setting committee meets eight times a year and sets a target range for the federal funds rate, which is what banks charge each other overnight. In September 2026 it raised that range to 3.75% to 4%. That one rate ripples outward: savings APYs, card APRs, auto and personal loan rates, and (less directly) mortgage rates all follow it.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Nobody signs up for it; it happens to everyone with a loan, a deposit, or a job. Borrowers with variable rates (cards, HELOCs, some student loans) feel each move within a billing cycle or two. Savers feel it when banks adjust, which is faster on the way down than on the way up.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The Fed doesn't make money off you. Banks do, in the gap between how quickly they pass rate rises to your loans and how slowly they pass them to your savings. The lag is where the margin lives.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Reading a rate decision as a prediction of what comes next; the committee says what it did, not what it will do. Locking a long-term rate the day before a cut, or carrying a variable balance into a hike. Assuming mortgage rates move with the Fed; they track longer-term bond yields and often go the other way.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is this rate fixed or variable? If variable, what is it tied to and how fast does it reset? What happened to this product's rate after the last Fed move? Where does the next decision date fall relative to my decision?

C2.title: High-yield savings account
C2.summary: Same account, 10 to 50 times the rate, usually from an online bank with no branches to pay for.
C2.hook: Same savings account. Ten to fifty times the interest. The difference is a building.
sources: FDIC National Rates and Rate Caps (national average savings rate 0.38%

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A savings account that pays a much higher interest rate, often 10 to 50 times a traditional bank's rate. Usually offered by online-only banks that have no branches to pay for.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: People holding an emergency fund or saving for something within the next few years who want the money to earn something while staying safe and reachable.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Same model as any bank, with a smaller cut. The rate is also a marketing tool: it moves with the Federal Reserve's rates and some banks trim it quietly once you've moved money in.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: The rate is variable and can drop. Transfers to your main bank can take 1 to 3 business days. Some accounts have tiers or caps on what earns the headline rate.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is this FDIC insured? Is the rate the same on the whole balance, or only up to a cap? How long do transfers take? Has this bank's rate held up over the last year?

C3.title: APY vs interest rate
C3.summary: APY is what you actually earn once interest earns interest. Always compare APY to APY.
C3.hook: Two accounts, same rate, different earnings. The letter that explains it is Y.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The interest rate is the plain percentage. APY (annual percentage yield) is what you actually earn in a year once interest is paid on interest, called compounding. APY is always equal to or slightly higher than the rate. For borrowing, the equivalent number is APR, which has its own card.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone comparing two savings accounts or CDs. APY is the number that lets you compare apples to apples.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Marketing. Ads lead with whichever number looks better. For savings they show APY (bigger); for loans they'd rather you not look at APR at all.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Comparing one account's rate to another's APY and picking wrong. Also mistaking a short promotional APY for the ongoing one.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is this number APY or rate? Is it promotional, and for how long? What's the APY after the promo ends?

C4.title: FDIC insurance
C4.summary: Government guarantee on deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank. Covers deposits, not investments.
C4.hook: The logo on the app is not the same as the guarantee on your money.
sources: SEC Investor Bulletin: SIPC Protection Part 1 · https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/investor-bulletin-sipc-protection-part-1-sipc-basics · 2023-06-07

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A government guarantee that if your bank fails, you get your money back, up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per account category. Credit unions have the same thing under a different name (NCUA). It covers deposits like checking, savings, and CDs. It does not cover investments.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone with a bank account, automatically, as long as the bank is a member. Nearly all U.S. banks are.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: It doesn't. Banks pay premiums into the fund. The thing to watch is companies that aren't banks (some fintech apps, some crypto platforms) using the FDIC logo loosely. Their coverage, if any, runs through a partner bank and can have gaps.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Assuming an app is a bank. Keeping more than $250,000 at one bank in one name. Confusing "FDIC insured" (deposits) with "SIPC" (brokerage accounts, which protect against the broker failing, not against investments losing value).

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is this company itself an FDIC-insured bank, or does it hold my money at a partner bank? Which partner? Does coverage apply if the app, not the bank, goes under?

C6.title: Insurance basics
C6.summary: Health, renters, auto, term life: what each actually covers, what a deductible is, and how premiums are set.
C6.hook: Insurance is the one thing you buy hoping to never use.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: You pay a premium each month, and if a covered bad thing happens, the insurer pays for it, after you pay the deductible. Health, auto, renters or homeowners, and term life are the ones most people need at some point. Each has a limit on what it pays and a list of what it doesn't cover.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Health: nearly everyone. Auto: required by every state and every lender. Renters: anyone renting, and it's cheap. Term life: people with someone who depends on their income.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Premiums are priced so that, across all customers, the insurer takes in more than it pays out. Riders, low deductibles, and add-ons raise the premium more than they raise the coverage. Whole life and other investment-style policies carry high commissions, which is why they're sold hard.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Being underinsured on the big things (liability, health) and overinsured on the small ones (phone, extended warranties). Not knowing the deductible until the claim. Letting a policy lapse and finding out the gap isn't covered.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the deductible and what's the maximum it pays? What specifically is excluded? Is this term or permanent life insurance, and why? What does the same coverage cost from two other companies?

C7.title: HSA
C7.summary: A health savings account with three tax breaks, and why some people treat it as a retirement account.
C7.hook: The only account where the money goes in untaxed, grows untaxed, and comes out untaxed.
sources: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-19 via IFEBP: 2026 HSA limits $4

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A savings account tied to a high-deductible health plan. Contributions skip income tax, growth isn't taxed, and withdrawals for medical costs aren't taxed either: three breaks, where a 401(k) or Roth gets two. In 2026 the limits are $4,400 for one person and $8,750 for a family. Unlike a flexible spending account, the balance rolls over forever and goes with you when you change jobs.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: People on a high-deductible plan through work or the marketplace. Some use it as a checking account for copays. Others pay medical bills out of pocket, invest the HSA, and keep the receipts, treating it as a second retirement account that happens to be medical.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The bank or custodian running the account charges a monthly fee, pays little interest on the cash portion, and often requires a minimum cash balance before you can invest the rest. Some charge for the investment menu too. Employers pick the custodian; you can move the money to another one.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Spending it on something that isn't a qualified medical cost, which brings tax plus a penalty before 65. Leaving years of contributions in cash. Not realizing the high-deductible plan itself can cost more if you need a lot of care that year. Losing receipts for the expenses you meant to reimburse later.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is my health plan HSA-eligible? What does the custodian charge, and what's the cash minimum before investing? Does my employer contribute anything? If I leave this job, can I move the account?

C8.title: Certificate of deposit
C8.summary: Lock money up for a set term for a set rate. The penalty for leaving early is the product.
C8.hook: The bank pays you more to promise you won't ask for it back.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A certificate of deposit: you hand the bank a sum for a set term (three months to five years) at a rate fixed for the whole term. At the end you get the sum back plus the interest. Take it out early and you pay a penalty, usually a few months of interest. Covered by FDIC insurance like any deposit.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: People with money they know they won't touch for a while and who want a rate locked in. Common for a house down payment a year out, or a chunk of an emergency fund past the first few months. Also popular with anyone who doesn't trust themselves not to dip into savings.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The bank lends your locked-up money out at a higher rate and keeps the difference, same as any deposit, but a CD lets it plan because it knows the money stays. The early-withdrawal penalty is the product: it's what makes the higher rate possible. Many CDs auto-renew at whatever the rate is that day, which is often lower than the one you signed up for.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Needing the money early and eating the penalty. Locking a long term right before rates go up and watching savings accounts pass you. Missing the renewal window and getting rolled into a worse rate. Chasing a promo rate at a bank you'll never use again.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the penalty, in months of interest? What happens at maturity if I do nothing? Is this rate fixed for the whole term? How does it compare to a plain high-yield savings account right now, and what am I giving up for the difference?

C9.title: Money market fund
C9.summary: Looks like savings, is actually an investment fund. Not FDIC insured, and that difference matters.
C9.hook: It looks like a savings account. It's an investment fund. One of them is insured.
sources: SEC Investor Bulletin: money market funds are not FDIC insured; the Reserve Primary Fund fell below $1.00 per share in September 2008 · https://www.sec.gov/investor/alerts/mmf-investoralert.htm · 2026-10-26
against the failure of a brokerage

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A mutual fund that holds very short-term, high-quality debt (Treasury bills, bank paper) and tries to keep its share price at exactly $1.00 while paying out the interest. Brokerages use them as the default place for uninvested cash. It's an investment, so it is not FDIC insured; if the brokerage fails, SIPC covers custody, not the value.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone with cash sitting at a brokerage, often without knowing it. Also people who want a savings-like yield on money they'll invest soon, and businesses parking payroll.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The fund charges an expense ratio, taken out of the yield before you see it. Brokerages often pay a lower sweep rate on your idle cash than their own money market fund yields, and they keep the gap unless you move the cash into the fund yourself.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Assuming it's insured. In 2008 one large fund's price dropped below $1.00 and investors lost money, which is why the SEC rewrote the rules afterward. Confusing a money market fund with a bank's money market account, which is a deposit and is insured. Not noticing the expense ratio on a fund whose entire return is a few percent.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is this a fund or a bank account? What's the expense ratio? What does it hold: Treasuries only, or bank and corporate paper? What's the yield after fees compared with my bank's savings rate?

D1.title: Credit score
D1.summary: A three-digit guess at how likely you are to repay. Built from your history, sold by bureaus, and yours to dispute.
D1.hook: You have several credit scores, not one, and three companies sell them.
sources: Capital One: Understanding types of credit scores (FICO and VantageScore ranges) · https://www.capitalone.com/learn-grow/money-management/understanding-types-of-credit-scores/ · 2024-10-24
AnnualCreditReport.com (free reports from all three bureaus) · https://www.annualcreditreport.com · 2026-10-23

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A three-digit number, usually 300 to 850, that lenders use to guess how likely you are to pay back what you borrow. Built from your history: whether you pay on time, how much of your available credit you use, how long you've had accounts, and how often you apply for new ones. The most common versions are FICO and VantageScore, and you have several scores, not one.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone who will ever rent an apartment, get a phone plan, finance a car, or take a mortgage. Employers and insurers sometimes check it too.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) sell your data to lenders. "Free credit score" apps are usually paid by the cards and loans they show you next to your score. Paid "credit monitoring" is often selling what you can get free by law.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: A low score makes every loan cost more, sometimes for years. Errors on your report are common and are yours to dispute. Checking your own score does not hurt it; a lender's "hard pull" when you apply does, a little.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Which score is this (FICO? Vantage? which version)? What's dragging it down: late payments, high utilization, short history? When did I last pull my free reports from the three bureaus?

D10.title: Debt payoff math
D10.summary: Avalanche versus snowball, minimum payments, and how long a balance actually takes to clear.
D10.hook: The minimum payment is a number designed to keep you paying.
sources: Federal Reserve G.19 via FRED: interest rate on credit card accounts assessed interest

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The arithmetic of getting out of debt. Two numbers decide it: the rate and how much more than the minimum you pay. At a 22% card rate, paying only the minimum on a balance can take well over a decade and cost more in interest than the original purchases. Every card statement is required to show you this calculation.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone carrying a balance on more than one thing: cards, a BNPL plan, a car, a student loan. The question is which to pay down first.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Lenders earn on the balance, so the longer it lasts the more they make. The minimum payment is set low enough to keep the balance alive for years. Debt-relief companies charge fees for plans you can usually set up yourself.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Paying extra on the lowest-rate loan first. Consolidating into a new loan and then running the cards back up. Not noticing a 0% promo ending and interest charging back from day one.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the rate on each balance? What's the minimum on each, and what happens if I put the extra on the highest rate first versus the smallest balance first? How long does the statement say this balance takes at the minimum?

D2.title: Credit card
D2.summary: Borrow with each purchase, pay in full and owe no interest. Pay less and you're carrying one of the priciest loans around.
D2.hook: The minimum payment is set exactly where it is for a reason. The reason is not you.
sources: Federal Reserve G.19 via FRED: interest rate on credit card accounts assessed interest

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A card that lets you borrow from the card company each time you buy something. You get a bill once a month. Pay the full balance by the due date and you pay no interest. Pay less than that and interest starts on what's left, at a rate that's usually among the highest of any common loan.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Most adults. Used in full each month, it's a convenient way to pay that builds credit history and sometimes earns rewards. Used as a loan, it's expensive.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Three ways: interest on balances you carry (the big one), a fee the store pays on every swipe (which funds rewards), and annual or late fees. Rewards programs are designed to work only if you spend more, and they're funded by people who carry balances.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: The minimum payment. It's set low enough that a balance can take years and cost more in interest than the original purchase. Also: a card is not an emergency fund, though it gets used as one.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the APR, and is there a different one for cash advances? Is there an annual fee? What's the grace period? If I only paid the minimum, how long would this balance take to clear (the statement has to tell you)?

D3.title: APR
D3.summary: The yearly cost of borrowing. A 24% APR on $1,000 carried for a year is about $240.
D3.hook: Most people with a card balance can't name their APR within ten points.
sources: Federal Reserve G.19 via FRED: interest rate on credit card accounts assessed interest

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percentage. It's the borrowing twin of APY. The average rate on cards that carried a balance was about 22% in August 2026. At 24%, a $1,000 balance carried for a year costs roughly $240 in interest, charged a bit each day. Loans with fees fold those fees into APR, which is why APR is the number to compare across lenders.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone with a card, a car loan, a mortgage, a student loan, or a BNPL plan. It's on every one of them, by law.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: It is how they make money. The trick is where it's shown: big for the 0% promo, small for what comes after. "Variable" APR means it moves when the Federal Reserve moves rates, which is most cards.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Not knowing yours. Promotional 0% periods that end and sometimes charge back interest from day one ("deferred interest") if any balance remains.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the APR after any promo? Fixed or variable? Is this "0% APR" or "no interest if paid in full," which is a different and worse thing?

D4.title: Buy now, pay later
D4.summary: Four payments over six weeks at checkout. The store pays the fee; you pay if you miss one or stack five plans.
D4.hook: Four easy payments. The store pays the fee. So who's the product?

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Splitting a purchase into a few payments, typically four over six weeks, offered at checkout by companies like Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay, and increasingly by card issuers themselves. The short "pay in 4" plans usually charge no interest. Longer plans for bigger purchases often do.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Online shoppers, heavily under 35, and increasingly for groceries and everyday items, which is what regulators watch.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The store pays the BNPL company a fee (often 2 to 8% of the sale) for the extra sales it drives. You pay late fees if you miss an installment, and interest on the longer plans. The business model depends on people buying more than they would have with one payment.

fields.short: Stacking: four or five plans running at once across different apps, with no single bill. Affirm began reporting all its plans to Experian in April 2025, and FICO released score versions that include BNPL data in late 2025, so these plans are starting to show up on credit files. Returns and refunds get messy when the merchant and the lender are different companies.

fields.short: Is this plan 0%, and what's the APR if not? What's the late fee? Does this report to credit bureaus, and does paying on time help or only hurt? How many of these do I have open right now?

D6.title: Student loans
D6.summary: Federal versus private, how interest accrues while you're in school, and what the repayment plans really cost.
D6.hook: The loan you signed at 18 has two versions, and the difference is thousands of dollars.
sources: Federal Student Aid: interest rates for Direct Loans first disbursed July 1

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Money borrowed for school. Federal loans come from the government with a fixed rate set each year (6.52% for undergraduates in 2026-27), income-based repayment options, and no credit check. Private loans come from banks, with rates set by your credit and fewer ways out if things go wrong.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: About half of people who finish a four-year degree, and plenty who don't finish. Parents too, through PLUS loans, which carry the highest federal rate.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Interest. On an unsubsidized loan it starts accruing the day the money is sent, while you're still in school, and gets added to the balance when repayment begins. Servicers are paid by the government to collect; private lenders keep the spread between what they borrow at and what they charge you.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Not knowing which type you have, because the rules are different. Interest capitalizing during a deferment. Missing that federal loans have income-based plans and private ones usually don't. Refinancing federal loans into private ones and losing those protections for a slightly lower rate.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Are these federal or private? Subsidized or not? What's the rate on each loan, and is interest accruing right now? Who is the servicer, and what repayment plans am I eligible for?

D7.title: Car loans
D7.summary: Why the dealer asks about the monthly payment first, and how a longer term hides a higher price.
D7.hook: The dealer asks what you can afford per month. That question is the sales tactic.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A loan to buy a vehicle, with the vehicle as collateral: miss payments and it can be repossessed. You pay the price plus interest over a set term. In early 2026 the average new-car loan was about $44,000 at $770 a month over 69 months, and more than a third of new loans ran longer than six years.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Most people who buy a car. Dealers arrange many of these loans on the spot, often through their own lender partners.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Interest, and the term. Stretching a loan from 60 to 84 months lowers the monthly payment and raises the total you pay, which is why the conversation starts with the payment, not the price. Dealers can also earn a markup on the rate they arrange for you, and sell add-ons (warranties, protection plans) rolled into the loan.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Being underwater: owing more than the car is worth for the first few years, which is nearly guaranteed on a long loan with a small down payment. Negotiating the payment instead of the price. Not knowing the rate until the paperwork.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the total price of the car, and what's the APR? What's the term? What would the payment be at a shorter term? Is there a rate from my own bank or credit union to compare against before I sit down?

D8.title: Mortgage & PMI
D8.summary: The biggest loan most people take, the insurance you pay when you put less than 20% down, and what escrow is.
D8.hook: Thirty years, one signature, and a fee for not having a fifth of the price in cash.

15-year fixed 6.68% for the week of October 22
CFPB: when can I remove private mortgage insurance (Homeowners Protection Act: request cancellation at 80% of original value

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A loan to buy a home, secured by the home. Most are fixed for 15 or 30 years; in late October 2026 the average 30-year rate was 7.32% and the 15-year 6.68%. Put down less than 20% on a conventional loan and the lender adds private mortgage insurance (PMI), a monthly charge that protects the lender, not you. Escrow is the extra each month the lender collects to pay your property tax and homeowner's insurance.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Most homebuyers. First-time buyers are the ones most likely to pay PMI, because 20% of a house price is a lot of cash. FHA and VA loans have their own versions of mortgage insurance with different rules.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Interest over decades: on a 30-year loan the first years' payments are mostly interest. Then origination fees, points, and closing costs at the start. PMI is pure margin for the lender's risk. Servicers also earn float on the escrow balance they hold.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Shopping by monthly payment and ignoring the rate and fees behind it. Not knowing PMI can be removed: by law you can ask once the loan hits 80% of the original value, and it drops automatically at 78%. Escrow shortfalls when taxes or insurance rise, which show up as a payment jump. Stretching to the maximum the lender approves.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the APR, including fees, not just the rate? What's the total I'd pay over the life of the loan? When does PMI come off, and do I have to ask? What's in the escrow estimate, and what happens when it's short?

D9.title: Refinancing
D9.summary: Replacing a loan with a cheaper one, when the closing costs make it worth it, and when they don't.
D9.hook: A lower rate is the headline. The closing costs are the fine print, and the clock restarts.
sources: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey: 30-year fixed 7.32%
15-year fixed 6.68% for the week of October 22

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Replacing an existing loan with a new one, usually to get a lower rate, a shorter term, or cash out of home equity. The new loan pays off the old one. You pay closing costs again (appraisal, title, origination), and on a mortgage the amortization clock starts over, so early payments go back to being mostly interest.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Homeowners when rates fall below what they locked in. Also people consolidating debt into a home loan, and student-loan borrowers moving to a private lender. In a 7% mortgage environment like late 2026, fewer people have a rate worth refinancing out of.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The lender earns fresh origination fees and points, and a brand-new 30-year interest schedule. 'No-closing-cost' refinances roll the costs into the balance or a higher rate. Cash-out refinances turn unsecured debt into debt secured by your house.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Refinancing for a small rate drop and never staying long enough for the savings to cover the costs. Resetting a 30-year loan with 20 years left and paying more total interest despite the lower rate. Refinancing federal student loans into private ones and losing income-based repayment and forgiveness options. Cashing out equity to pay off cards, then running the cards back up.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What are the total closing costs, and how many months of savings does it take to recover them? Will I still be here then? What's the total interest on the new loan versus finishing the old one? For student loans: what federal protections am I giving up?

I1.title: 401(k) match
I1.summary: Employer money you only get if you contribute. Vesting decides when it's really yours.
I1.hook: Part of your salary is sitting in a drawer at HR, and you only get it if you ask.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A 401(k) is a retirement account offered through an employer. Money goes in from your paycheck before it reaches you. A match is when the employer adds its own money on top, usually a formula like "50% of what you put in, up to 6% of your pay" or "100% of the first 3%, then 50% of the next 2%." The match is part of your pay that you only get if you contribute.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Employees whose company offers one. Not every job does, and some require a waiting period before the match kicks in.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The plan provider charges fees, often buried in the funds inside the plan (see Expense ratio). Some plans have good, cheap fund menus; some have bad, expensive ones, and you can't shop around because your employer picked it.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Leaving the match on the table. Not knowing the vesting schedule: the employer's contributions may not fully belong to you until you've stayed a certain number of years. Early withdrawals before 59½ generally mean taxes plus a 10% penalty.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the match formula, exactly? When am I fully vested? What funds are in the plan and what do they cost? Is there a Roth option inside it?

I10.title: Diversification
I10.summary: Not putting it all in one place. What it protects against, and what it doesn't.
I10.hook: It's not about owning more things. It's about owning things that don't all fall on the same day.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Spreading money across investments that don't move together: many companies instead of one, several industries, more than one country, stocks and bonds rather than only stocks. The point is that one bad outcome, a company failing or a sector collapsing, doesn't take the whole account with it. A broad index fund is diversification in one purchase.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone, including people who think they're diversified because they own ten tech stocks. Also the employee whose retirement account is heavy in their own company's shares, which puts their paycheck and their savings on the same bet.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Diversification itself is free. Products sold under its name aren't: overlapping funds that each charge a fee while holding the same stocks, 'alternative' investments with high costs and lockups pitched as diversifiers, and advisors charging to assemble what one fund already does.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Owning twelve funds that all hold the same large U.S. companies. Thinking it protects against a market-wide drop; it doesn't, it protects against a single-name drop. Mistaking it for a guarantee against loss. Diversifying so far into obscure things that fees eat the benefit.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: If my biggest holding went to zero, what would happen to the account? How much overlap is there between these funds? How much is in my employer's stock? What's the one thing that, if it went wrong, would hurt everything I own at once?

I11.title: Dollar-cost averaging
I11.summary: Investing a fixed amount on a schedule regardless of price. What it does to your average cost, and what it doesn't.
I11.hook: Same amount, same day each month, no matter the price. The math is modest. The habit is the point.
sources: 'Cost averaging: Invest now or temporarily hold your cash?' (lump sum came out ahead of a 3-month cost-averaging plan about two-thirds of the time

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule regardless of what the market is doing. When prices are low the amount buys more shares; when high, fewer. Anyone contributing from each paycheck into a 401(k) is already doing it. The alternative, for a lump sum, is investing it all at once.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Most people, by default, because money arrives in paychecks. Also people who received a lump sum (bonus, inheritance, sale) and are nervous about putting it all in the day before a drop.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Nobody charges for the idea. Brokers do earn more when it's done in small frequent trades with spreads or commissions on each one, and apps built around 'round-ups' and micro-investing often charge flat monthly fees that are a large percentage of a small balance.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Treating it as a way to beat the market. Vanguard's research found that for a lump sum, investing it all at once came out ahead of spreading it over three months about two-thirds of the time, because markets have risen more often than fallen. Cost averaging reduces regret, not expected return. Stopping the schedule during a drop, which is the moment it does the most.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Am I doing this because money arrives monthly, or because I'm nervous about a lump sum? What does each purchase cost me in fees or spread? If the market fell by a third next month, would I keep the schedule?

I12.title: Dividends
I12.summary: Cash a company pays holders, how it's taxed, and why a high yield can be a warning rather than a gift.
I12.hook: A dividend isn't free money. The share price drops by the same amount the morning it's paid.
sources: Dividends: qualified dividends taxed at the 0%
or 20% capital gains rates; ordinary dividends at regular income rates · https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc404 · 2026-10-26

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Cash a company pays out to shareholders from its profits, usually quarterly. The yield is the annual dividend divided by the share price. On the day a dividend is paid, the share price drops by about that amount; the money moved from the company's account to yours. In a taxable account, 'qualified' dividends are taxed at the lower capital-gains rates; others at regular income rates.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone who owns stocks or stock funds gets them, often reinvested automatically. Retirees sometimes build portfolios around them for income. Dividend-focused funds and 'high-yield' strategies are marketed heavily to people who want cash flow without selling shares.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The company doesn't profit from paying you. Funds built around dividends charge expense ratios like any other, and some 'income' products use options or leverage to manufacture a high payout while the underlying value erodes. Tax is the quiet cost: dividends in a taxable account are taxed the year they're paid whether you wanted the cash or not.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Chasing a high yield without asking why it's high; often the share price has fallen because the business is in trouble and the dividend is about to be cut. Thinking dividends are extra return on top of price gains. Holding dividend payers in a taxable account when a retirement account would shelter them.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Why is this yield higher than similar companies? Has the dividend ever been cut? Is it qualified for tax purposes? Am I holding this in the right kind of account? What's the total return including price, not just the yield?

I13.title: Rebalancing
I13.summary: Selling what grew to buy what shrank, back to your target mix. How often, and why it feels wrong.
I13.hook: Sell some of what went up. Buy some of what went down. It feels wrong every single time.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Bringing a portfolio back to its intended mix after markets move it. If the plan was 70% stocks and 30% bonds and a good year made it 78/22, rebalancing sells some stock and buys bonds to get back to 70/30. It's done on a calendar (once a year), on a trigger (when the mix drifts by a set amount), or by directing new contributions to whatever is under target.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone with more than one kind of investment. Target-date funds and robo-advisors do it automatically; that's a large part of what they charge for. People managing their own 401(k) often never do it, which is how a retirement account quietly becomes all stocks.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Each trade can carry a spread or commission, and in a taxable account selling a winner triggers capital gains tax. Services sell automatic rebalancing as a feature worth an ongoing fee, when a once-a-year calendar reminder does most of it.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Never doing it, so risk creeps up during booms and the account is at its riskiest right before a fall. Doing it too often and paying taxes and spreads for tiny adjustments. Rebalancing in a taxable account when it could be done free inside the 401(k). Abandoning the plan during a crash, when rebalancing means buying the thing that just dropped.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What mix did I set out to hold, and what is it now? Can I rebalance with new contributions instead of selling? Which account can I do this in without triggering tax? When did I last check?

I14.title: Risk tolerance
I14.summary: How much drop you can sit through without selling. A behavior, not a questionnaire score.
I14.hook: Everyone is a long-term investor until the account is down 30%.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: How much of a drop you can sit through without selling. It's a behavior, discovered in a real decline, not a score from a ten-question quiz. It has two parts people conflate: capacity (how much loss your life can absorb: time until you need the money, stability of income) and tolerance (how much you can stomach). A twenty-five-year-old has high capacity and may still have low tolerance.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Every investor, whether they've named it or not. Brokerages and advisors ask about it on sign-up because regulators require them to match what they sell to what the client can bear.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The questionnaire is free. What's sold on the back of it isn't: 'conservative' portfolios heavy in high-fee products, annuities pitched to anyone who checked 'I worry about losses,' and advisory fees for managing anxiety rather than money. Panic-selling in a crash is the most expensive thing most people ever do, and someone is on the other side of that trade.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Answering the questionnaire in a calm year and finding out the answer in a bad one. Confusing a long time horizon with a strong stomach. Holding all stocks because that's what 'aggressive' people do, then selling at the bottom. Holding all cash because a drop once scared you and losing decades to inflation.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: How much did a portfolio like this fall in 2008 and in 2020, in dollars, not percent? What would I have done? When do I need this money? If it dropped by a third tomorrow, what's my plan, written down now?

I15.title: Valuation basics
I15.summary: P/E, market cap, and the other numbers on a quote page, and what each one can and can't tell you.
I15.hook: The quote page has a dozen numbers. Two of them matter, and neither tells you what to do.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The numbers on a stock quote page and what they mean. Market cap: share price times shares outstanding, the total price of the company. P/E ratio: price divided by a year's earnings per share, roughly how many years of profit you're paying for. Earnings per share, revenue, dividend yield, and 52-week range fill out the rest. None is a verdict; each is a measurement.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone who looks at an individual stock. Analysts and fund managers run deeper versions. Most index-fund investors never need them, and that's fine; the numbers matter for understanding what you own, not for timing anything.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The data is free. What's sold is interpretation: stock-picking newsletters, screeners with premium tiers, 'undervalued stock' lists, and courses that teach a formula as if it were a secret. Brokers benefit when the numbers prompt trading.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Comparing P/E across industries where normal ranges differ wildly. Treating a low P/E as 'cheap' when it may mean the market expects earnings to fall. Looking at share price alone, which says nothing without the share count. Mistaking a story about a company for its numbers, or the numbers for the whole story.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the market cap, and what business is actually worth that much? What's the P/E, and what's typical for this industry? Are earnings growing or shrinking? What would have to be true for this price to make sense?

I16.title: Bond yields
I16.summary: Why bond prices fall when rates rise, what a yield curve is, and why people watch its shape.
I16.hook: When rates go up, the bond you already own goes down. Here's why that's not a contradiction.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A bond's yield is what it pays relative to its price. Prices and yields move opposite: if new bonds pay more, nobody pays full price for an old one paying less, so its price falls until the two match. The yield curve plots yields of government bonds from short to long maturity. Normally longer bonds pay more. When short-term yields rise above long-term, the curve is 'inverted,' which has often come before recessions and is watched for that reason.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone with a bond fund, including most target-date and balanced funds. Savers comparing CDs to Treasuries. Homebuyers, indirectly: mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield more than they track the Fed.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Bond funds charge expense ratios. Brokers earn a markup (the spread) on individual bonds that doesn't show up as a commission. Rising rates cost bond holders through price drops; falling rates cost savers through lower yields. Banks live in the gap between short rates they pay depositors and long rates they lend at.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Learning that bonds can lose money the year it happens, as many did in 2022. Buying a long-term bond fund for 'safety' when it has more rate risk than a short one. Reading an inverted curve as a certain forecast; it's a signal with a mixed record, not a schedule.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the duration of this bond fund, and what does that mean if rates rise one point? What's the yield after the expense ratio? Is this a Treasury or corporate bond, and what's the default risk? What's the 10-year yield doing, and why do I care?

I17.title: Leverage
I17.summary: Borrowing to invest or trade. Multiplies gains and losses alike, and the broker gets paid either way.
I17.hook: Borrowed money doubles the gain and doubles the loss. The lender gets paid either way.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Using borrowed money to control more of an investment than your cash alone would buy. Margin loans at a broker, leveraged ETFs that aim for two or three times an index's daily move, options and futures, and a mortgage on a rental property are all forms. Gains and losses both scale with the borrowed amount; the loan and its interest don't shrink when the asset does.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Traders, by design. Everyday investors, often by accident: a leveraged ETF bought because it was 'the 3x version,' or a margin loan taken to avoid selling. Real estate investors use it deliberately, with the property as collateral.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Interest on the borrowed amount, charged daily, in good markets and bad. Leveraged ETFs carry higher expense ratios and lose value over time from the daily reset even when the index goes nowhere. Brokers collect margin interest and can force-sell your positions at the worst moment to protect their loan.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Losing more than you put in. A margin call that sells you out at the bottom. Holding a daily-reset leveraged fund for months and getting a return nothing like three times the index. Treating leverage as a way to catch up after a loss.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What am I paying to borrow, and what return does the investment need to cover it? What's the worst case, in dollars? Who decides when I'm sold out, and at what level? Is this fund designed to be held for one day or one year?

I18.title: Withdrawal rates
I18.summary: How much a portfolio can pay out each year without running dry, and where the famous 4% came from.
I18.hook: The famous 4% came from one planner, one spreadsheet, and the worst years of the 1960s.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: How much a retirement portfolio can pay out each year without running dry. In 1994 a financial planner named William Bengen tested every 30-year stretch since 1926 and found that a first-year withdrawal of 4% of the portfolio, raised each year for inflation, had survived all of them, including the stretch beginning in the late 1960s. That's the origin of 'the 4% rule.' It's a historical finding about a 50/50 stock-bond mix, not a law.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone planning to live off savings, and anyone trying to figure out how much savings that takes. Advisors, planning software, and retirement calculators all build on some version of it.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The research is public. The industry around it sells certainty: annuities marketed as the answer to running out, advisory fees for a withdrawal plan, and 'income' products with high costs. Guaranteed-income pitches target exactly the fear this topic raises.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Treating 4% as safe for any portfolio, any time horizon, any market. A bad first few years (sequence risk) hurts far more than the same bad years later. Withdrawing a fixed amount from an all-stock portfolio. Ignoring taxes: a withdrawal from a traditional IRA is income; from a Roth it isn't.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What mix is this portfolio, and what time horizon am I planning for? What happens to the plan if the first three years are bad? Which accounts do I draw from first, and what's the tax on each? What's my plan to adjust if the balance falls?

I19.title: Estate basics
I19.summary: Beneficiaries, wills, and why the form you filled out at the bank can override the will.
I19.hook: The form you filled out when you opened the account beats the will you paid a lawyer to write.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: What happens to your accounts and property when you die. A will covers things that don't already have a named recipient. Retirement accounts, life insurance, and many bank and brokerage accounts pass by beneficiary designation, the form on file with the institution, and that form overrides the will. Property with no clear path goes through probate, a court process that is public, slow, and costs money.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone with an account or a dependent, which is everyone. Especially anyone who has married, divorced, or had a child since they opened an account; the beneficiary form doesn't update itself.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Probate fees, attorney fees, and in some states a percentage of the estate. Institutions charge nothing for a beneficiary form, which is why it's the single highest-value piece of paperwork in personal finance. Estate-planning packages and trusts are sold to people whose situation a form and a simple will would cover.

fields.short: An ex-spouse still named on the 401(k). No beneficiary at all, which sends a retirement account through probate and can trigger a faster, larger tax bill for heirs. A minor named directly, who can't legally receive it. Nobody knowing where the accounts are.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Who is the beneficiary on each of my accounts, right now? Is there a contingent? Does anyone I trust know what accounts exist? What in my situation actually needs a will or a trust, and what's already handled by the forms?

I2.title: Roth vs traditional
I2.summary: Two tax timings for the same account: pay tax now or pay it later. A label, not a product.
I2.hook: Roth and traditional are not two products. They're one account with two tax calendars.
sources: NerdWallet: 2026 Roth IRA contribution and income limits ($7

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Two tax treatments that apply to retirement accounts (both 401(k)s and IRAs). Traditional: money goes in before tax, grows untaxed, and you pay income tax when you take it out. Roth: money goes in after tax, grows untaxed, and comes out tax-free. Same account, different timing of the tax. An IRA is the version you open yourself, not through work, with lower annual limits.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone saving for retirement in a tax-advantaged account has to pick one, and the choice turns on tax rates now versus later, which nobody knows for sure.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The accounts themselves don't. Brokerages earn on what's inside them and on cash sitting uninvested. Some providers charge IRA account fees; many charge none.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Thinking it's a product rather than a tax label. Contributing to a Roth IRA when income is above the limit. Treating "tax-free later" as free: Roth contributions cost you the deduction today.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is my income likely higher or lower now than it will be in retirement? What are this year's contribution limits? I3.title: Index fund
I3.summary: One purchase, a slice of everything on a list. Cheap because nobody is paid to pick.
I3.hook: One purchase, 500 companies, and nobody getting paid to guess.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A fund that buys a whole list of investments at once, matching an index like the S&P 500 (500 large U.S. companies) rather than trying to pick winners. One purchase gives you a small slice of everything on the list. Comes in two wrappers: a mutual fund (priced once a day) or an ETF (trades like a stock during the day).

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Most first-time investors and a large share of professionals. It's the default inside many 401(k)s and robo-advisors.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The expense ratio, which is small by design, often 0.03 to 0.20% per year. That's the whole pitch: it's cheap because no one is being paid to pick stocks. Some brokers also earn on the cash in your account or on "payment for order flow" when you trade.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: It goes down when the market goes down, fully. There's no manager stepping in. Historically broad markets have recovered, but over years, not weeks, and past results don't guarantee future ones. Also: not all "index funds" track broad indexes; some track narrow or gimmicky ones with higher fees.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What index does it track? What's the expense ratio? Is there a sales charge ("load") or a minimum? Is this a mutual fund or an ETF, and does that matter for how I'd buy it?

I4.summary: The fund's yearly fee, taken automatically. The one number known in advance, and it compounds against you.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of what you have in it, taken out automatically so you never see a bill. 0.05% means $5 a year on $10,000. 1.00% means $100. fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: This is the fee. It's how fund companies, and often the advisor or plan that put you in the fund, get paid. Because it's a percentage, it grows with your balance for the rest of your life.

I5.title: Compound growth
I5.summary: Returns on returns. Works for you in a fund and against you on a card balance. Starting early beats starting big.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Earning returns on your returns. Money that grows 7% in year one is a bigger pile in year two, so 7% of that is more dollars, and so on. Over long periods the curve bends upward. It works the same way in reverse on debt: unpaid interest gets added to the balance and then earns interest itself.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone, whether they mean to or not. Savers and investors benefit from it; people carrying card balances are on the other side of it.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The idea is free. But it's the engine behind both the expense ratio (a small fee compounding against you for decades) and credit card APR. Anyone selling you something will show compounding working for you and skip where it's working against you.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Expecting it to feel like much in the first few years. It doesn't; the dramatic part comes late, which is why time in the market has mattered more than the size of the first deposit. And mistaking a projection ("at 7% a year") for a promise. Returns are not steady. Broad U.S. stocks have averaged roughly 6.5 to 7% a year after inflation over two centuries, with long stretches well above and below that, and none of it is a guarantee.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What rate is this projection assuming, and is it after fees? Over how many years? What does the same math say about my debt?

I7.title: Stocks vs bonds
I7.summary: Ownership versus lending. Why one swings more, and why most portfolios hold both.
I7.hook: One is owning. The other is lending. Everything else is detail.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A stock is a slice of ownership in a company: you get a share of its profits if it does well and nothing promised if it doesn't. A bond is a loan to a company or government: they pay you a set interest rate and give the money back at the end. Stocks swing more and have historically returned more; bonds swing less and pay less.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Nearly every investment account holds some of each, usually through funds. The mix is what people mean by how risky a portfolio is.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Stocks: the company earns on your money, not off you, but the fund or broker you hold it through charges fees. Bonds: the borrower pays you interest; the middlemen earn on the spread and on fund fees.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Thinking bond prices only go one way (they fall when rates rise). Holding all stocks and selling in the first drop. Holding all bonds for decades and losing ground to inflation.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the mix of stocks and bonds in what I own? How much did a portfolio like this fall in the last bad year? What am I being paid to lend, and to whom?

I8.title: ETF vs mutual fund
I8.summary: Two wrappers for the same holdings: one trades all day, one prices once. What that changes for you.
I8.hook: Same fund, two wrappers. The difference is when you can buy it and what it costs to hold.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Two ways to package the same basket of investments. A mutual fund is bought and sold once a day at that day's closing price, often with a minimum investment. fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Paying a load on a mutual fund when a near-identical ETF has none. Trading an ETF often because you can. Buying an ETF at a thin moment and paying a wide spread.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is there a sales charge or a minimum? What's the expense ratio for each version? Does this fund distribute capital gains every year? If I'm in a 401(k), which wrapper does the plan actually offer?

fields.short: A single fund that holds a mix of stocks and bonds and shifts toward bonds as a chosen year (2055, 2060) approaches. You pick the year closest to when you'd retire and it rebalances itself. It's the default option in many 401(k) plans and held $4.8 trillion in 2025.

M1.title: Scams & red flags
M1.summary: Guaranteed returns, urgency, and payment by gift card. The patterns, so you recognize the next variation.
M1.hook: Every scam has the same three parts. Learn the shape and the version doesn't matter.
sources: FTC: reported fraud losses reached about $16 billion in 2025; imposter scams $3.5 billion · https://ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/06/ftc-data-show-people-reported-losing-3-point-5-billion-imposter-scams-2025 · 2026-06-15

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Someone getting you to send money or information by pretending to be something they're not. People reported about $16 billion in fraud losses in 2025, a record, with $3.5 billion of that from imposters posing as a bank, a government agency, a company, or a relative. fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone, and increasingly younger adults, who report losing money more often than older ones. Nobody thinks they're the target until they are.

fields.short: The scam is the product; the whole thing is how it makes money off you. The three parts: a promise or a threat (guaranteed returns, your account is compromised, a relative in trouble), urgency (act now, don't tell anyone), and an untraceable payment (wire, crypto, gift cards, a payment app to a stranger).

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Acting before checking. Trusting caller ID, an email address, or a voice (all can be faked). Sending a second payment to recover the first, which is its own scam. Not reporting it because of embarrassment.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Can I hang up and call the organization back at the number on my card or statement? Why does this need to happen right now? Why this payment method? Would a real bank, agency, or employer ever ask for this?

M2.title: Fintech "banks"
M2.summary: Apps that look like banks but aren't. Where your money actually sits, and what happens if the app fails.
M2.hook: The app has a debit card and a routing number. It is not a bank, and the difference showed up in 2024.
sources: Banking With Third-Party Apps: deposit insurance covers bank failure

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Apps that offer checking-like accounts, cards, and savings but aren't banks themselves. They hold your money at a partner bank behind the scenes, often through a middleman that keeps the ledger of whose money is whose. The FDIC insures the bank; it does not insure the app or the middleman. If the app or its ledger-keeper fails, getting your money back depends on how good their records were.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Younger customers, people frustrated with bank fees, gig workers who get paid through the app, and anyone who signed up for a high promotional rate. Many don't know they aren't at a bank.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Interchange fees every time you swipe the card, interest on your deposits that the partner bank shares with the app, subscription tiers, instant-transfer fees, and sometimes the sale of your transaction data. The 'no fees' pitch means no monthly fee; it doesn't mean free.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: The middleman failing. In 2024 a ledger company between several apps and their banks collapsed, and customers were locked out for months while regulators tried to reconstruct who was owed what. Thinking 'FDIC insured' on the app's website means the app is insured. No branch and a chatbot when something goes wrong. Account freezes with no human to call.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Which bank actually holds my money? Is the account in my name at that bank, or in the app's name? What happens to my money if the app shuts down? How do I reach a person?

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: An automated investing service: answer a questionnaire, get a portfolio of low-cost index funds matched to it, and the service rebalances and (on some tiers) tax-loss harvests for you. fields.short: The advisory fee, every year, on the whole balance, regardless of performance. Some keep a cash allocation that earns the firm interest. Premium tiers add human advisors and higher fees. The underlying funds charge their own expense ratios on top.

fields.short: Paying 0.25% a year for what a single target-date or balanced fund does for less. Multiple accounts across multiple robos, each with its own fee. M4.title: AI money tools

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Chatbots and apps that answer money questions, categorize spending, or suggest what to do with cash. Some are general assistants; some are built into banks, brokers, and budgeting apps. fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Nearly everyone now, often without noticing: the 'ask us anything' box in a banking app, the budgeting assistant, the chatbot a friend screenshots. People use them for exactly the questions they're embarrassed to ask a person.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: If it's inside a product, the product's incentives are its incentives: a bank's assistant explains the bank's accounts, a broker's assistant is comfortable with trading. Standalone tools earn through subscriptions, data, or referrals to the things they mention. An answer that ends with a specific product to open is a sales channel, whatever it calls itself.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Trusting a number it stated with confidence and never checking it. Giving it account details it stores. Taking a recommendation from something that isn't licensed to give one and has no liability if it's wrong. Mistaking fluency for accuracy.

fields.short: Who made this and how do they make money? Is it telling me what something is, or what I should do? Where did that number come from, and can I find the source? What did I just give it, and where does that go?

M6.title: Crypto & stablecoins
M6.summary: Tokens, exchanges, wallets, and what a stablecoin is actually backed by. The custody risk nobody explains.
M6.hook: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins. If that's an exchange, you own an IOU.
sources: 2025): payment stablecoin issuers must hold 1:1 reserves in cash and short-term Treasuries and publish monthly reserve reports · https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/1582 · 2025-07-18

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Digital tokens recorded on a blockchain, a shared ledger no single company controls. Bitcoin and ether are the largest. A stablecoin is a token meant to hold a fixed value, usually one dollar; since a 2025 federal law, U.S. payment stablecoin issuers must back each token one-for-one with cash and short-term Treasuries and publish monthly reports. You hold crypto either in your own wallet (you control the keys) or at an exchange (they do).

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Traders, people moving money across borders, people who distrust banks or their government's currency, and a lot of people who bought because a price was going up. Stablecoins are used for trading pairs and, increasingly, for payments.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Exchanges charge trading fees, spreads, withdrawal fees, and earn interest on the cash and stablecoins customers leave with them. Stablecoin issuers keep the interest on the reserves; the token pays you nothing. 'Yield' programs lend your coins out and keep part of the return, with your coins as the thing at risk.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: An exchange failing with customer coins inside; several have. Losing the keys to a self-custody wallet, which is permanent. Sending to a wrong address, which is also permanent. Tax: every swap between coins is a taxable sale. Scams, which are over-represented here because payments can't be reversed.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Where are my coins held, and who controls the keys? If this exchange failed tomorrow, what would I be? What backs this stablecoin, and where's the report? What's the total fee on a round trip in and out? Have I recorded every trade for taxes?

M7.title: Tokenized assets
M7.summary: Stocks and real estate on a blockchain. What's real, what's a wrapper, and who holds the underlying thing.
M7.hook: A token that says 'one share of a company' is a claim on whoever is holding the actual share.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Traditional assets (stocks, Treasuries, real estate, funds) represented as tokens on a blockchain. The token usually isn't the asset; it's a claim on an asset that a company holds in custody somewhere. The pitch is 24-hour trading, fractional ownership, and faster settlement. The question is always what sits behind the token and what legal rights the holder has to it.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Early adopters, crypto traders who want exposure to stocks without leaving their platform, overseas investors reaching U.S. assets, and institutions testing settlement systems. Still a small corner of the market.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Issuance and redemption fees, trading spreads on thin markets, and custody fees on the underlying asset. Some tokens don't pass through dividends or voting rights, so the issuer keeps what the real shareholder would get.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Discovering the token conveys a contract with the issuer, not ownership of the share, when the issuer gets into trouble. Thin liquidity: a price that exists on screen but not when you try to sell. Regulatory status that's still being worked out, with products that may be pulled from U.S. customers. Paying a premium over the real asset's price for the convenience.

fields.short: What exactly do I own: the asset, or a claim on a company that holds it? Who's the custodian and who audits them? Do I get the dividends and votes? What happens if the issuer fails? What does the same asset cost in a regular brokerage account?

M8.title: Prediction markets
M8.summary: Betting on events, priced as probabilities. How the odds are set and why they're not quite forecasts.
M8.hook: The market says 62%. That's a price, set by people with money on the line. It's not quite a forecast.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Markets where you buy and sell contracts that pay out if an event happens: an election result, a Fed decision, a sports outcome. A contract trades between zero and one dollar, and its price is read as the crowd's probability. The platforms are regulated in the U.S. as exchanges for event contracts; the legal line between this and gambling is still being argued in court and state by state.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Traders, political junkies, hedgers (someone whose business depends on a rate decision), and journalists quoting the odds. Volume spikes around elections and big economic releases.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Trading fees, a spread between buy and sell prices, and interest on the cash you deposit while you wait for a contract to resolve. Like any exchange, the house earns on volume, not on which side wins.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Reading the price as a forecast when it reflects who's betting and how much; a thin market can be moved by one large trade. fields.short: Who's on the other side of this, and why? How much volume is behind this price? What exactly counts as 'yes,' and who decides? What are the fees on a round trip? Do I know something about this outcome that I'm not allowed to trade on?

P10.title: Capital gains tax
P10.summary: What you owe when you sell something for more than you paid, and why holding a year changes the rate.
P10.hook: Hold it 366 days instead of 365 and the tax rate on the gain can drop by half or more.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The tax on the profit when you sell something for more than you paid: stocks, funds, crypto, property. Held a year or less, the gain is 'short-term' and taxed like wages. Held more than a year, it's 'long-term' and taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income. For 2026 the 0% rate covers taxable income up to $49,450 single or $98,900 married filing jointly. Losses offset gains. None of this applies inside a 401(k), IRA, or HSA.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone who sells an investment in a taxable account. Also people selling a home (there's a large exclusion for a primary residence), a business, or collectibles (which have their own rate).

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The government is the one collecting, but the cost shows up where you don't expect: mutual funds that pass capital gains to holders every year whether or not you sold; frequent trading that turns long-term gains into short-term ones; tax software that upsells for investment forms. Brokers report your cost basis, and mistakes there are yours to fix.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Selling at eleven months when another month would have cut the rate. Forgetting that reinvested dividends raise your cost basis, and paying tax twice. Not knowing a fund's distributions are taxable in a taxable account. Trading crypto between coins and not realizing each swap is a sale.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: How long have I held this? What's my cost basis, and does the broker have it right? What bracket does this gain land in? Would this be taxed differently inside a retirement account? Do I have losses that could offset it?

P11.title: Tax-loss harvesting
P11.summary: Selling a loser to offset a winner's tax bill, and the wash-sale rule that trips people up.
P11.hook: Sell the loser, bank the loss against the winner, buy something almost identical. Wait 31 days or it doesn't count.
sources: Capital Gains and Losses: net capital losses offset up to $3
30 days before or after the sale · https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550 · 2026-10-26

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Selling an investment that's down to realize the loss on paper, then using that loss to offset gains elsewhere, which cuts the tax bill. Losses beyond your gains can offset up to $3,000 of regular income a year, with the rest carrying forward. The catch is the wash-sale rule: buy the same or a 'substantially identical' investment within 30 days before or after the sale and the loss is disallowed.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: People with taxable brokerage accounts and gains to offset. Robo-advisors sell automated versions as a premium feature. Useless inside a 401(k) or IRA, where gains aren't taxed anyway.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The tax benefit is real but it's a deferral, not a gift: the replacement investment has a lower cost basis, so the gain shows up later. Robo-advisors and advisors market it as a return-enhancer worth their fee. The IRS collects when the wash-sale rule is broken by accident.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Rebuying the same fund inside the window, including automatically through dividend reinvestment or a 401(k) contribution to the same fund, which triggers the rule across accounts. Selling a position just for the loss and missing a rebound while sitting in cash. Doing it in a year with no gains and a low bracket, where the loss is worth little.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What gains do I have this year to offset? What will I hold instead, and is it 'substantially identical'? Do any of my other accounts buy this same fund automatically? What's the new cost basis, and when will that gain come due?

P2.title: Gross vs net pay
P2.summary: Gross is what you earned. Net is what landed. Offers and loan applications use gross; your budget runs on net.
P2.hook: A $25-an-hour job does not put $1,000 in the bank for a 40-hour week. Here's where the rest went.

fields.short: Gross pay is what you earned before anything is taken out. Net pay is what actually lands in your account. The difference is taxes and deductions.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone who gets a paycheck, and everyone who's ever been surprised that a $25/hour job doesn't put $1,000 in the bank for a 40-hour week.

fields.label: How it makes money off you

fields.label: What goes wrong

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's my net per paycheck? Which deductions are required (taxes) and which did I choose (retirement, insurance)?

P3.summary: Money sent to the government out of each check: federal, FICA, and state where it applies. A big refund was your money all along.

P5.title: Checking account
P5.summary: The account money moves through. Built for spending, not growing, so it pays almost nothing.

fields.short: The bank account money moves through: pay comes in, bills and purchases go out. Comes with a debit card. It's built for spending, not for growing money, so most pay little or no interest.

fields.label: Who ends up using it

P6.title: Overdraft
P6.summary: Spending more than you have. The bank declines it or covers it and charges a fee, historically $30 to $35 each.
P6.hook: The $35 fee for having $4 in your account.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Spending more than is in your checking account. The bank either declines the transaction or covers it and charges an overdraft fee, often around $35 per occurrence. Several large banks dropped the fee in 2021 and 2022 and others cut it to about $10; many still charge the full amount.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Nobody on purpose. It happens most to people living paycheck to paycheck, which is why it's been the subject of so much regulation.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The fee itself. Overdraft and NSF fees ran about $5.8 billion in 2023, down from $12.6 billion in 2019. A federal rule capping the fee at $5 at large banks was finalized in December 2024 and repealed by Congress in May 2025, so the fee is back to whatever each bank sets. "Overdraft protection" is a product you opt into that covers the shortfall from a linked account, sometimes for a smaller fee.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Several fees in one day from small purchases. Some banks have reordered transactions largest-first, which triggers more overdrafts.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Am I opted in to overdraft coverage, or will the card just decline? What's the fee, and is there a daily cap? Can I link savings as a backstop instead?
