P7.title: Emergency fund
P7.summary: Cash kept separate for the car repair or the job gap. A concept, not a product, and nobody is selling it.
P7.hook: The only money idea with nobody selling it.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Cash kept separate from spending money, meant for things like a car repair, a medical bill, or a gap between jobs. It's a concept, not a product: it usually lives in a savings account.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone whose income could stop or whose expenses could spike, which is nearly everyone. People without one tend to end up on credit cards or overdraft when the surprise comes.

fields.label: How it makes money off you

P8.title: Budget basics
P8.summary: Where the net pay goes each month, and the handful of methods people actually stick with.
P8.hook: A budget isn't a diet. It's a map of where the money already goes.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A plan for where each paycheck goes before it arrives: bills, saving, spending. Any method works if you look at it monthly. fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone whose money runs out before the month does, and anyone who has no idea what they spent last month. That's most people the first time they try it.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The idea is free. The apps around it are not: budgeting apps charge monthly fees or sell you the products they show next to your spending. A spreadsheet or your bank's own category view does the same job for nothing.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Making one so detailed it dies in week two. Budgeting on gross pay instead of net. Treating it as a one-time setup instead of a monthly check. Forgetting the once-a-year bills that land all at once.

P9.title: Side income & 1099
P9.summary: Getting paid without withholding: what you owe, when, and the quarterly payments nobody mentions.
P9.hook: Nobody withheld anything. That's not a bonus. That's a bill arriving in April.
sources: IRS Form 1040-ES (2026): self-employment tax 15.3% (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare); estimated payments due April 15

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Money earned outside a regular paycheck: freelancing, gig apps, a small business, selling things. It arrives with no tax withheld, and you owe both income tax and self-employment tax (15.3%, which is both halves of Social Security and Medicare that an employer would otherwise split with you). The IRS expects it paid through the year in four estimated payments, due around April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Anyone with a 1099 instead of a W-2: drivers, contractors, consultants, creators, resellers. Also W-2 employees with a side project that crosses a few hundred dollars of profit.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The IRS charges a penalty for underpaying through the year, even if you pay in full in April. Platforms take their cut before you see the money and then report your gross to the IRS. Tax software charges extra for the self-employment forms. Bookkeeping and 'business formation' services sell structure most small side incomes don't need.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Spending all of it and meeting the tax bill in April. Not tracking expenses, which are deductible and reduce both taxes. Missing the quarterly dates. Not knowing that half the self-employment tax is itself deductible. Assuming a loss-making hobby can offset a salary.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: How much of each payment do I set aside? What expenses count against this income? Do I owe estimated payments this year? What did the platform report, and does my own record match it?

T1.title: Order types
T1.summary: Market, limit, stop. What each one promises, and when a market order costs you.
T1.hook: 'Buy' isn't an order. It's three different orders, and one of them can fill at a price you never saw.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Instructions to a broker. A market order says 'get me in now at whatever the price is.' A limit order says 'only at this price or better,' and may never fill. A stop order sits dormant until the price hits a trigger, then becomes a market order, which is how a stop set to limit a loss can fill well below the trigger in a fast move. A stop-limit adds a floor, at the cost of maybe not filling at all.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone who places a trade, including people who only ever hit the big green button, which is usually a market order. Active traders use limits by default.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Market orders fill at the ask (buying) or the bid (selling), so you pay the spread every time. Brokers that sell your order flow to market makers earn more on market orders because those are the easiest to profit from. The fees are invisible; they show up as a slightly worse price.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: A market order on a thinly traded stock or ETF at the open, filling far from the last price you saw. A stop-loss triggered by a brief dip, selling you out right before the rebound. A limit set so tight it never fills while the price runs away. Not knowing which type the app's default button is.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What type of order is this button? What's the spread right now? If I use a stop, what happens in a gap down? Is this order good for the day or until cancelled?

T10.title: Futures
T10.summary: Contracts on a future price, built-in leverage, and why they were invented for farmers, not traders.
T10.hook: Invented so a farmer could lock in a price before harvest. Now mostly traded by people who've never seen a bushel.
sources: CME Group: the Chicago Board of Trade was founded in 1848 and standardized grain futures contracts in 1865 · https://www.cmegroup.com/company/history/timeline-of-achievements.html · 2026-10-26

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A contract to buy or sell something at a set price on a future date: grain, oil, gold, a stock index, interest rates. Standardized futures date to Chicago in the 1860s, built so farmers and millers could fix a price ahead of harvest. Today most volume is financial. You post a small deposit (margin) against a much larger contract, so leverage is built in, and gains and losses are settled to your account every day.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Producers and big users hedging real exposure: farmers, airlines, refiners, pension funds. Speculators providing the other side. Retail traders through 'micro' contracts and through ETFs that hold futures (most commodity funds work this way).

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Exchange and broker fees per contract, interest on the margin deposit the broker holds, and the daily spread. Funds that hold futures pay a 'roll' cost each time a contract expires, which can quietly erode returns even when the commodity price is flat.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Leverage that turns a small move into a wipeout and a margin call. Holding a contract into delivery. Buying an oil ETF, watching oil rise, and losing money anyway because of roll costs. Not understanding that losses are debited nightly, not at the end.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the full contract value, not just the margin? What does a one-percent move do to my account? When does this expire and what happens then? If this is a fund, what's the roll cost been over the past year?

T11.title: Backtesting
T11.summary: Testing a strategy on past data, and the overfitting trap that makes every backtest look great.
T11.hook: Every strategy looks great on the data it was built from. That's not a result. That's a mirror.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Running a trading rule against past prices to see how it would have done. Useful for finding out whether an idea is nonsense; dangerous because of overfitting: tweak the rules enough and any strategy will fit history perfectly and fail going forward. The honest version tests on data the rule never saw, includes trading costs and spreads, and counts the strategies that were tried and discarded.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Quant funds, with teams and skepticism. Retail traders and the people selling to them, usually with a chart of a line going up and to the right.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Backtesting software subscriptions, 'proven' systems sold on their historical curve, signal services, and algorithmic-trading courses. The curve in the ad was chosen from many; you're paying for the survivor.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Fitting the rule to the data and calling it a discovery. Leaving out costs, slippage, and the stocks that went bankrupt and dropped out of the database. Testing on ten years that happened to be a bull market. Trading real money on a backtest with no out-of-sample period.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Was any of this data held back and tested after the rule was fixed? Are spreads, commissions, and taxes included? How many versions were tried before this one? What happens to the curve if I start it a year later?

T2.title: Bid-ask spread
T2.summary: The gap between the buy and sell price. The quiet fee on every trade, biggest where volume is thinnest.
T2.hook: There are two prices for everything. You buy at the higher one and sell at the lower one. The gap is the fee.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: The difference between the highest price a buyer will pay (the bid) and the lowest a seller will accept (the ask). Buy at the ask, sell at the bid, and you've lost the spread before anything moves. On a heavily traded stock or ETF it's a penny; on a small company, a niche ETF, an option, or a crypto token it can be a percent or more. It's widest at the open, the close, and in a panic.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Everyone who trades, every time. Index investors pay it rarely; day traders pay it constantly, which is a large part of why frequent trading is expensive even with zero commissions.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Market makers earn the spread: they buy at the bid, sell at the ask, and pocket the difference thousands of times a day. Brokers that route your orders to those market makers are paid for sending them. 'Commission-free' moved the cost from a line item into the spread.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Trading a thin ETF because it had the right name and paying a wide spread each way. Placing a market order on an option and filling at the far edge of a wide spread. Not noticing the cost because it never appears as a fee. Day-trading a small account where spreads alone eat the gains.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the bid and ask on this right now, and what's that as a percent? How much does this trade a day? What time is it, and is the spread wider than usual? If I bought and sold this instantly, what would I lose?

T3.title: Volatility
T3.summary: How much a price moves, how it's measured, and why it's priced into everything on this line.
T3.hook: Volatility isn't risk of losing money. It's how big the swings are. The two get confused on purpose.
sources: Cboe: the VIX Index measures the market's expectation of 30-day volatility implied by S&P 500 option prices · https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/vix/ · 2026-10-26

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A measure of how much a price moves, up or down, over time, usually stated as an annualized percentage. Historical volatility looks back; implied volatility is what option prices suggest traders expect ahead. The VIX, often called the fear index, is the implied 30-day volatility of the S&P 500. Options cost more when volatility is high, because bigger swings make them more likely to pay.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Options traders live by it. Everyone else feels it: a high-volatility fund is the one whose statements are hard to open. Risk-scoring tools and 'conservative' portfolio labels are mostly volatility measurements.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Products sold on volatility: VIX-linked funds that lose value over time by design, 'low-volatility' funds with higher fees than a plain index, and option strategies pitched as income that are short volatility and blow up when it spikes. Brokers earn more when volatility rises because people trade more.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Buying a VIX product as a long-term hedge and watching it decay. Mistaking a calm stretch for safety and a volatile one for danger; some of the best buying days in history were the scariest. Selling options for 'income' without understanding that the premium is pay for taking the big-swing risk.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the volatility of this, and what has that meant in dollars over a bad month? Is this product long or short volatility? Is it designed to be held for a day or a decade? What happens to it when the VIX doubles?

T4.title: Technical vs fundamental
T4.summary: Charts versus financials. What each approach claims, and what the evidence says about both.
T4.hook: One camp reads the charts. One reads the financials. The record says most of both trail an index.
sources: SPIVA U.S. Scorecard (year-end 2025): most actively managed U.S. equity funds trailed their benchmark over 15 years · https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/research-insights/spiva/ · 2026-03-15

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Two schools of picking what to buy. Technical analysis studies price and volume patterns on charts, on the theory that past movement predicts future movement. Fundamental analysis studies the business: earnings, debt, growth, competition, on the theory that price eventually follows value. Most professional managers use the second; most retail trading apps are built around the first.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Traders use technicals. Analysts and long-term investors lean fundamental. Most people mix them without naming either. Course sellers and chart-pattern influencers target beginners with the first because it looks learnable in a weekend.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Charting platforms, data subscriptions, trading courses, signal services, and newsletters, most priced monthly. Brokers earn when either method produces trades, and technical analysis produces far more of them.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Seeing patterns in noise. The long-running SPIVA scorecards find most professional stock pickers, with teams and data, trail a plain index fund over 15 years; a retail trader with a pattern and a phone is unlikely to do better. Paying for a course that teaches what's free. Confusing a strategy that worked in a bull market with one that works.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the evidence this method beats an index after costs? Who's selling it to me and what do they earn? How would I know if it stopped working? What's my result over the last two years compared to just holding a broad fund?

T5.title: Margin
T5.summary: Borrowing from your broker to buy more. The interest, the margin call, and who decides when you're sold out.
T5.hook: The broker lends you money to buy more, charges interest daily, and decides when to sell you out.
sources: Margin Regulation: Regulation T initial margin 50%; FINRA maintenance margin 25% of market value · https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/key-topics/margin-accounts · 2026-10-26

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Borrowing from your broker against the investments in your account to buy more. Federal rules let you borrow up to half the purchase price; brokers require you to keep at least 25% equity after that, and most set a higher bar. Fall below it and you get a margin call: add cash or the broker sells your holdings, at its choice of which and when.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Active traders by design. Ordinary investors sometimes by accident, when an app enables margin by default or offers 'instant buying power.' Some use margin loans as a cheap way to borrow against a portfolio without selling.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Interest on the loan, compounded daily, often at rates well above a mortgage. The broker also earns by lending out the shares you bought on margin to short sellers, and from the extra trading margin encourages. A forced sale in a crash is executed to protect the broker's loan, not your position.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: A 30% drop in a fully margined account is a 60% drop in your equity, plus a margin call at the bottom. The broker selling the position you'd have kept. Not realizing margin was on. Using it to average down into a falling stock.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Is margin enabled on this account, and did I ask for it? What's the interest rate? At what price would I get a call, and what happens if I don't answer the phone? What's the worst case in dollars?

T6.title: Short selling
T6.summary: Betting a price falls by selling what you borrowed. Why the loss is unlimited and the borrow has a fee.
T6.hook: Buy low, sell high, in the other order. The most you can make is 100%. The most you can lose has no limit.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Betting on a price falling. You borrow shares through your broker, sell them, and plan to buy them back cheaper to return. If the price falls, the difference is yours. If it rises, you owe the difference, and there's no ceiling on how high a price can go. You pay a borrow fee while the position is open and owe any dividends the stock pays.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Hedge funds, professional traders, and market makers hedging. Retail investors occasionally, usually on a stock they're angry at, and more often through inverse ETFs, which short for you with their own costs.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The broker charges a borrow fee that can be small or enormous on hard-to-borrow names, plus margin interest, since shorting requires a margin account. The broker also earns by lending your long shares to other shorts. Inverse ETFs carry high expense ratios and daily-reset decay.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: A short squeeze: a rising price forces shorts to buy back, which pushes it higher, which forces more buying. Unlimited loss, which margin calls make real. Being right about a company and still losing because the timing was off. Borrow fees that quietly exceed any gain.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: What's the borrow fee today, and can it change? What's the most I can lose, and is there a number at all? What happens to this position if the stock doubles overnight? Do I owe the dividend?

T8.title: Options basics
T8.summary: Calls, puts, premium, expiry. Why so many short-dated options expire worthless, and who collects the premium.
T8.hook: The buyer pays for the right to be right by a deadline. The seller collects the fee and waits for the clock.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: A contract on 100 shares. A call is the right to buy at a set price (the strike) before a set date (expiry); a put is the right to sell. The buyer pays a premium for that right. The seller collects the premium and takes on the obligation. Options lose value as expiry approaches, so a buyer needs to be right about direction, size, and timing; the seller is paid for the buyer's chance of missing one of them.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Professionals, for hedging and income. Retail traders, in large numbers since commissions went to zero, mostly buying short-dated calls on the apps that make it feel like a game. Covered calls (selling calls against stock you own) are the common 'income' version.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: The premium flows from buyers to sellers, and sellers as a group have a structural edge because time is on their side. Brokers earn on every contract, and options order flow is far more valuable to market makers than stock order flow, so apps push options hard. Spreads on options are wide, especially on far-out strikes.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Buying short-dated options because they're cheap and watching them go to zero in a week. Selling 'naked' calls with unlimited loss. Getting assigned on a short put and owning stock you didn't budget for. Treating a 10x story as the typical outcome rather than the rare one.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: Am I the buyer or the seller here, and what's my maximum loss? What has to happen, by when, for this to profit? What's the spread on this contract? Does the app earn more when I trade options than stock?

T9.title: Position sizing
T9.summary: How much to put in any one trade. The math that keeps one bad call from ending the account.
T9.hook: The question isn't what to buy. It's how much. Get that wrong and being right doesn't matter.

fields.label: What it is
fields.short: Deciding how much of the account goes into any one position. The usual framing: how much would I lose if this is wrong, and what fraction of the account is that? Traders often cap the loss per trade at a small fixed fraction of the account so that a string of losses, which happens to everyone, can't end it. The size follows from the distance to the exit, not from conviction.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.short: Every trader, and every investor who's ever put a large share of their money in one stock. The employee with most of their net worth in company shares has a position-sizing problem whether or not they trade.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.short: Nobody charges for the idea; the cost of ignoring it is paid to the market. Brokers earn more from large, frequent, concentrated bets than from small careful ones, and app design (leaderboards, confetti, 'buying power') pushes toward the former.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.short: Betting big on a sure thing. Averaging down into a loser until it's most of the account. Sizing by how confident you feel instead of how much you'd lose. Surviving ten trades and being wiped out by the eleventh. Never writing down the exit before entering.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.short: If this goes against me, where do I get out, and what's that in dollars? What fraction of the account is that? How many losses in a row could I survive? Is this size based on the math or on how sure I feel?
